question.text: Does patient-prosthesis mismatch after aortic valve replacement affect survival and quality of life in elderly patients?
question.context: To evaluate the impact of patient-prosthesis mismatch (PPM) on survival, functional status, and quality of life (QoL) after aortic valve replacement (AVR) with small prosthesis size in elderly patients. Between January 2005 and December 2013, 152 patients with pure aortic stenosis, aged at least 75 years, underwent AVR, with a 19 or 21 mm prosthetic heart valve. PPM was defined as an indexed effective orifice area less than 0.85 cm/m. Median age was 82 years (range 75-93 years). Mean follow-up was 56 months (range 1-82 months) and was 98% complete. Late survival rate, New York Heart Association functional class, and QoL (RAND SF-36) were assessed. Overall, PPM was found in 78 patients (53.8%). Among them, 42 patients (29%) had an indexed effective orifice area less than 0.75 cm/m and 17 less than 0.65 cm/m (11.7%). Overall survival at 5 years was 78 ± 4.5% and was not influenced by PPM (P = NS). The mean New York Heart Association class for long-term survivors with PPM improved from 3.0 to 1.7 (P < 0.001). QoL (physical functioning 45.18 ± 11.35, energy/fatigue 49.36 ± 8.64, emotional well being 58.84 ± 15.44, social functioning 61.29 ± 6.15) was similar to that of no-PPM patients (P = NS).

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The study found no significant difference in overall survival between patients with and without patient-prosthesis mismatch (PPM) after aortic valve replacement. While there was improvement in New York Heart Association functional class and QoL in patients with PPM, these improvements were not statistically significant compared to those without PPM. Therefore, the mismatch did not appear to negatively impact survival or QoL in this cohort of elderly patients.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: Overall survival at 5 years was 78 ± 4.5% and was not influenced by PPM (P = NS).
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: While the study found improvements in QoL and functional status in patients with PPM, it's possible that these improvements were not clinically significant or that other factors influenced these outcomes. However, the lack of a significant impact on survival makes this less likely.
